summary: Lars Fogelin works in Indology, Buddhist studies, and archaeology. He earned his PhD at the University of Michigan (1995–2003) under Carla Sinopoli and held posts at Albion College, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, and the University of Arizona.

Lars Martin Fosse is an Indologist and linguist. He studied at the University of Oslo (~1973–1984), Heidelberg University, and the University of Bonn, later teaching at the University of Oslo (attested 2002).

Lati Rinpoche (1922–2010) was a scholar in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and philosophy. Educated at Ganden Shartse, Ganden, and Gyuto monasteries, he served as abbot of Ganden and Ganden Shartse (~1976–1985) and visiting scholar at the University of Virginia (~1976).
Latika Lahiri (b. 1923) is a scholar of Sinology and Buddhist studies. She studied at Peking University under Xianlin Ji in 1958 and held a post at the University of Delhi from ~1969 to 1988.

Laura Harrington specializes in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and religious studies. She completed her studies at Columbia University, where she was supervised by Robert A. F. Thurman and taught by Ryuichi Abe, Theodore Riccardi Jr., and Gary A. Tubb, among others.

Lauran Hartley is a Tibetologist who has held positions as an adjunct lecturer at Columbia University, visiting assistant professor at Indiana University, teacher at Rutgers University (attested 2003), and consultant and editor at the Latse Contemporary Tibetan Cultural Library (attested 2003).

Laurence Austine Waddell (1854–1938) studied medicine at the University of Glasgow (~1874–1878) and worked in Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and archaeology. He served in the Indian Army and Medical Service, taught at Kolkata's Medical College, and was Professor of Tibetan at UCL (1906–1908).

Laurence Binyon (1869–1943), who worked in Sinology and Japanology, studied at Trinity College, Oxford (~1888–1892). He held long-term posts at the British Museum (~1893–1933) and Harvard University (~1933–1934).

Laurence Khantipalo Mills (1932–2021) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under teachers including Sangharakshita, Acharya Buddharakkhita, Dudjom Rinpoche, Jianmin Chen, and Namkhai Norbu. In 1978, he served as abbot at Wat Buddha Dhamma.

Laurie L. Patton (b. 1961) is an Indologist who earned a BA at Harvard and a PhD at Chicago. She held faculty and leadership roles at Emory, Duke, and Middlebury College, and became President of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (~2024).

Lawrence E. Sullivan is a religious studies scholar. He served as Director of the Center for the Study of World Religions (attested 2000), Professor at Harvard University (attested 2000–2004), and Professor of Theology at the University of Notre Dame (attested 2005).

Lawrence William Nelson specializes in Buddhist and religious studies. His extensive education includes studies at Butler, Indiana, New York, and Northwestern Universities, St. John's College, and a PhD and Religion degree from the California Institute of Integral Studies (attested 2012).

LeRoy Carr Barret (1877–1960) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Washington and Lee University (~1895–1898) and completed further studies under Maurice Bloomfield at Johns Hopkins University (~1899–1903).

Leah Zahler (b. 1936) is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Tibetology. She earned her PhD at the University of Virginia, where she studied under Jeffrey Hopkins (1980–1981), Harvey B. Aronson, and Ngawang Wangyal.

Leedom Lefferts specializes in Buddhist and religious studies. He served as Professor of Anthropology, Emeritus at Drew University (attested 2011) and as a Research Associate in the Department of Anthropology at the Smithsonian Institution (attested 2011).

Leela Aditi Wood works in Buddhist studies and archaeology. She earned her PhD at the University of Michigan (concluded 2005) under supervisors Luis O. Gómez and Martin J. Powers, and later held a post at Deccan College.

Leo Frobenius (1873–1938) was an archaeology scholar. He led the Frobenius Institute (1920–1938), taught at Goethe University Frankfurt (1932–1938), directed the Museum der Weltkulturen (1935–1938), and was active in the Berlin Society for Anthropology, Ethnology, and Prehistory.

Leo M. Pruden (1937–1991) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo (1964–1966) under Akira Hirakawa and Taitetsu Unno. He held posts at Brown University (1970–1971), Nyingma Institute (1971), and the University of Oriental Studies (attested 1988).

Leo Meyer (1830–1910) was a linguist who studied under Theodor Benfey, Franz Bopp, and Jacob Grimm at Göttingen and Berlin. He was a professor at the University of Göttingen and held the chair of comparative linguistics at the University of Tartu (1865–1899).

Leo Strauss (1899–1973) was a philosopher who studied at the universities of Marburg, Hamburg, Freiburg, and Columbia. His major academic posts included long tenures at The New School (~1938–1949), the University of Chicago (~1949–1969), and St. John's College (~1969–1973).
